primary_claim: SAE latents that appear to track a human-interpretable feature (e.g. 'starts with E') often fail to fire on examples that should trigger them, because other, more token-specific 'absorbing' latents causally take over in their place -- a phenomenon the authors term Feature Absorption, found using over 200 Gemma Scope SAEs on a first-letter identification task with ground-truth labels.

effect.metric: SAE latent classifier precision/recall vs linear probes on first-letter task

contradicts_or_qualifies: SAE latents that appear to classify a feature can be much worse/unreliable classifiers than linear probes, despite superficial interpretability
stated_future_work: Validating feature absorption: is it reduced in different SAE architectures?
Validating feature absorption: does it appear for other kinds of features?
Refining feature absorption metrics, such as removing the need to train a linear probe
Exploring strategies for mitigating feature absorption (e.g. Meta-SAEs, fine tuning against attribution sparsity)
Building better toy models and theories of feature absorption with co-occurring features
limitations_stated: our results use a leverage model (Gemma-2-2b), one SAE architecture (JumpReLU) and one task (the first letter identification task)
quote: SAE latents can appear to classify some feature of the input, but actually turn out to be quite unreliable classifiers (much worse than linear probes)
